Maintenance costs and security exposure on the old platform grow every year, and the engineers who understand it are approaching retirement. Some large customers threaten to switch vendors entirely if forced to migrate.

Plan the end-of-life and migration program for the legacy product. agentResponses.content:
# Legacy Product Sunset: The Profitability Paradox and the Architecture of Managed Decline

---

## The Actual Problem (Not What You Think It Is)

Let me be blunt about what's happening and why the obvious answer—"just sunset it"—will blow up in your face.

**You have a cash cow that's also a liability.** That's not a problem to solve quickly; it's a problem to solve *carefully*, because the moment you mishandle the transition, three things happen simultaneously:

1. **Your replacement product loses credibility.** The customers who defect aren't just leaving; they're broadcasting to the market: "Your company doesn't support customers through transitions; they force you to switch or leave." Word spreads. Your NPS tanks. Sales cycles lengthen.

2. **You lose the revenue floor.** One-third of your profit is not trivial. If you sunset aggressively and 30-40% of legacy customers defect (entirely realistic), you've just destroyed $X million in recurring revenue with nothing to replace it for 12-24 months. Your board will not forgive you.

3. **You create a competitive opening.** Competitors will position themselves as "the stable choice that doesn't force migrations." They'll target your legacy customers explicitly. Some will even acquire the legacy product from you or hire away your engineers to re-create it.

**The meta-lesson:** This isn't a technical problem. It's a *customer segmentation and retention problem masquerading as a product problem.*

The right answer is not "sunset the legacy product" but rather: **"Manage the decline of the legacy product while systematically upgrading customer cohorts to the replacement, on a timeline that preserves revenue and customer relationships."**

This takes 24-36 months, not 12 months. It's messier than a clean sunset. But it protects your business.

---

## Strategic Positioning: The Choice You Need to Make First

Before you design a sunset timeline, clarity on constraint.

You have three postures:

**Posture A: Aggressive Sunset (12-18 months)**
- Hard deadline for legacy product: "We will cease support on [date]"
- Force migration: No new features for legacy; minimal security patches; deprecation messaging
- Outcome: Revenue from legacy drops 40-60% within 6 months; 20-30% of customers churn entirely; replacement product growth accelerates (because it's now "the only choice")
- Cost: Relationship damage; competitive vulnerability; short-term revenue cliff
- Viable if: Your replacement product is feature-complete for 90%+ of your customer base AND you can absorb a 30-40% revenue drop for 6-12 months AND you're not in a competitive market

**Posture B: Managed Decline (24-36 months) [Recommended]**
- Soft sunset: "We're ending active development on legacy; security support continues; new features redirect to replacement"
- Segmented migration: Different timelines for different customer cohorts based on feature dependency
- Incentivized migration: Pricing, tooling, and support designed to make replacement more attractive than staying
- Outcome: Revenue from legacy declines gradually (30-50% over 24 months); 10-15% of customers defect entirely; replacement product gains most legacy customers; relationships preserved; competitive position intact
- Cost: Longer execution; more complex program management; dual-track support costs elevated for 2+ years; harder to celebrate "we sunsetted it"
- Viable if: You can tolerate gradual revenue decline AND you want to preserve customer relationships AND you have a competitive market where customer defection is costly

**Posture C: Strategic Maintenance (Indefinite)**
- No sunset. Legacy product enters "maintenance mode": security patches only; no new features; minimal engineering headcount
- Focus: Extract maximum margin from legacy while gradually migrating customers at their own pace
- Outcome: Legacy revenue stays relatively flat ($X million/year, declining 5-10%/year); customer relationships preserved; replacement product growth drives overall growth; you eventually stabilize at a state where legacy is 10-15% of revenue
- Cost: Perpetual maintenance burden; ongoing security risk; engineering team frustrated with maintaining "dead" product; difficult to retire the product entirely
- Viable if: Your legacy customers are sticky AND you have spare engineering capacity AND you can afford the security/maintenance overhead indefinitely

**My recommendation: Posture B** with the following assumptions:

- Your replacement product covers 85-95% of use cases in your customer base
- You have 10-20% of customers with high switching costs (either niche features or high integration depth) who would defect if forced immediately
- You can tolerate 24-36 months of dual-track support and engineering
- Your board will accept a gradual revenue decline from legacy if you can show a credible plan to migrate 70-80% of customers

If your replacement product covers <85% of use cases, start with Posture C and invest in closing the gaps before attempting any sunset.

---

## The Sunset Architecture: Posture B in Detail

Here's how to execute a managed decline that preserves revenue and relationships.

---

### **Phase 0: Diagnostic and Segmentation (Weeks 1-4)**

You can't migrate customers without understanding their dependencies.

#### **Action 0.1: Legacy Product Customer Segmentation (Days 1-7)**

Bucket your legacy customers by three dimensions: feature dependency, switching cost, and defection risk.

```
LEGACY CUSTOMER SEGMENTATION: EXAMPLE

Customer Cohort | Size | Annual Spend | Core Dependency | Niche Dependency | Replacement Coverage | Switching Cost | Defection Risk | Migration Timeline
---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---
**Pragmatists (Migration-Ready)** | 35% | Median $50K | Standard features in both products (reporting, integrations, core workflow) | None significant | 95%+ | Low (switching is easy) | Low (they see the replacement as "better") | 6-12 months
**Feature-Dependent (Stuck)** | 28% | Median $120K | Standard features | Niche feature X (e.g., custom API, deprecated workflow, legacy connector) | 70-80% | High (niche feature is critical to their ops) | High (will defect if forced) | 18-24 months (after feature rebuilt)
**Deep-Integrators (Embedded)** | 22% | Median $200K | Standard + custom integrations (APIs, webhooks, embedded solutions) | Custom integrations / API usage patterns | 60-70% | Very High (integrations would require engineering effort to rebuild) | Very High (will defect or demand heavy discounts) | 24-36 months (with significant tooling support)
**Vendor-Agnostic (Mercenaries)** | 10% | Median $75K | Price + feature parity | None | 90%+ | Low (they're platform-agnostic) | Medium-High (will defect if competitor undercuts you) | 12-18 months (incentive-driven)
**Holdouts (Die-Hard Legacy Advocates)** | 5% | Median $30K (declining) | Legacy-specific features (deprecated, not re-built) | Multiple niche features | <50% | Very High (organization culturally attached to legacy) | Very High (will likely never migrate; will defect eventually) | Not viable (accept churn)

---

**Diagnostic Insights by Cohort:**

**Pragmatists (35%)**
- These are your "easy wins." They use legacy product because it works, not because it's irreplaceable.
- Replacement covers everything they care about; some new features are actually better
- Risk: They're not motivated to migrate yet (legacy is "working fine"). Inertia is the barrier, not capability.
- Strategy: Light incentive + simple migration path + clear messaging that replacement is superior → 80-90% convert within 6-12 months
- Revenue impact: Minimal loss; these customers stay because replacement is actually better

**Feature-Dependent (28%)**
- These are your "critical sticking point." They depend on 1-3 niche features that the replacement doesn't have (yet).
- Without those features, they will defect rather than migrate
- Examples: Custom API endpoints, deprecated but critical integration, legacy data format, specific workflow automation
- Risk: They're the customers most likely to defect or demand heavy discounts
- Strategy: Rebuild the missing niche features in replacement (or find a workaround) BEFORE migrating them → Most convert within 18-24 months after features are available
- Revenue impact: High; losing this segment is costly. Rebuilding features is expensive. But not rebuilding features costs more (they all defect).

**Deep-Integrators (22%)**
- These customers have embedded legacy into their systems: custom integrations, API calls, embedded dashboards, white-label deployments
- The replacement exists, but the integration work to move them is substantial (100-500 hours of engineering effort per customer)
- Risk: They will demand heavy discounts or migrate to competitors rather than pay for migration
- Strategy: Build migration tooling (API bridge, data migration scripts, integration templates) to reduce their engineering burden → Most convert within 24-36 months if tooling is strong; otherwise 30-50% defect
- Revenue impact: Medium-High risk; these are your largest customers ($200K median) so losing even a few is costly

**Vendor-Agnostic Mercenaries (10%)**
- These customers use your product because it's the best option *at a given price point*. If competitor offers better deal, they leave.
- They have no moat; replacement is just as good as legacy; but they're price-sensitive
- Risk: If you don't incentivize migration, they'll shop around during the transition window
- Strategy: Aggressive pricing incentive for early migration to replacement ($X discount for Y-year contract) → 70-80% stay if incentive is strong enough
- Revenue impact: Low risk if incentivized; high risk if left alone (they migrate to competitor)

**Holdouts / Die-Hard Legacy Advocates (5%)**
- These are your "accept as churn" segment. They love the legacy product; they'll never voluntarily migrate; they'll resist any sunset.
- Rebuilding features for them is not cost-effective (they're only 5% of base; not worth the engineering cost)
- Risk: They WILL defect when you force the sunset. Expect 80-100% churn from this segment.
- Strategy: Accept their churn. Don't spend engineering effort on them. Let them go gracefully (offer 6-month free trial on competitor product, help them export data, etc.). Use them as a learning opportunity (why are they so loyal to legacy? What does replacement need to win over similar customers?)
- Revenue impact: Minimal (they're 5% of base; even 100% churn is only 5% of revenue)
```

**Key insights from segmentation:**

1. **Your real problem is not "should we sunset legacy" but "how do we rebuild the niche features that keep 28% of customers locked in?"** 

   The Feature-Dependent cohort (28% of base, $120K median) will not migrate without the niche features. If you don't rebuild them, you lose $336M in annual revenue (0.28 × $120K × 1000 customers, rough example). Rebuilding those features costs money, but it's far cheaper than losing 28% of your revenue.

2. **Your second problem is "how do we make migration easy for the Deep-Integrators?"**

   These are your largest customers ($200K median) and they have the highest switching costs. They won't defect because of missing features; they'll defect because migrating their custom integrations is too expensive/risky. Tooling (data migration scripts, API bridge, integration templates) can reduce that friction. This tooling is cheaper than losing 22% of your base.

3. **Pragmatists and Vendor-Agnostic are low-risk.** They'll migrate with light incentives and clear messaging. Don't over-invest in these segments; focus on Feature-Dependent and Deep-Integrators.

4. **Holdouts are a sunk cost.** Accept their churn. Don't waste engineering effort on them. They're 5% of your base; losing them is annoying but not catastrophic.

---

#### **Action 0.2: Feature Dependency Deep Dive (Days 3-10)**

For the Feature-Dependent cohort, identify exactly which niche features they depend on and whether rebuilding is viable.

```
FEATURE DEPENDENCY ANALYSIS: EXAMPLE

Niche Feature | # of Customers (Legacy) | Annual Revenue at Risk | Replacement Has Feature? | Rebuild Cost Estimate | Rebuild Timeline | Rebuild Priority | Strategic Value
---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---
**Custom API Endpoints (Deprecated)** | 12 | $1.2M | No; design is incompatible with replacement architecture | $150K (2 engineers, 12 weeks) | 12-16 weeks | High | Medium: Only niche use cases; could also solve with API bridge instead
**Legacy Data Format (XML Exports)** | 8 | $800K | Partial (replacement has JSON, CSV; missing XML) | $30K (1 engineer, 6 weeks) | 6-8 weeks | Critical | High: Easy rebuild; high ROI (30K cost, 800K revenue at risk)
**Deprecated Integration (FTP Upload Connector)** | 15 | $1.5M | No; replacement has S3, SFTP, HTTPS, but customers still on legacy FTP setup | $80K (1 engineer, 10 weeks) + $50K (infrastructure) | 10-14 weeks | High | High: Rebuild is low-effort; high ROI; customers just haven't upgraded their FTP setup (organizational inertia)
**Custom Workflow Automation (Deprecated)** | 6 | $1.2M | Partial (replacement has workflow engine, but different UX/logic) | $200K (2 engineers, 16 weeks) | 16-20 weeks | Medium | Low: Only 6 customers; 200K cost/1.2M at-risk = borderline ROI; but these are sticky customers; losing them is costly
**Legacy Report Format (Multi-column Custom Reporting)** | 5 | $750K | Partial (replacement has flexible reporting, but UX is different; requires 4-5 more clicks per report) | $120K (1 engineer, 12 weeks) | 12-16 weeks | Medium | Medium: High ROI but affects only 5 customers; however, these reports are critical to their business
**Embedded Dashboard Component (White-label)** | 3 | $600K | No; replacement has dashboard, but white-label is not available | $250K (1 engineer, 20 weeks + design + infra setup) | 20-24 weeks | Low | Low: Only 3 customers ($200K each); 250K cost is too high relative to customer base; better to offer these 3 customers custom services budget instead
**Real-time Data Feed (Deprecated API)** | 7 | $700K | Partial (replacement has webhooks; customers need real-time, but replacement's latency is slightly higher) | $180K (1 engineer, 14 weeks; performance optimization) | 14-18 weeks | High | Medium: 7 customers; rebuild is doable; moderate cost; high impact

---

**Prioritized Feature Rebuild List:**

**Tier 1: Must Rebuild (High ROI; Low Cost)**
1. Legacy Data Format (XML Exports): $30K cost; $800K at-risk; 6-8 week timeline → ROI ~26:1 → Do immediately
2. Deprecated Integration (FTP Upload Connector): $130K cost; $1.5M at-risk; 10-14 weeks → ROI ~11.5:1 → Do immediately
3. Real-time Data Feed: $180K cost; $700K at-risk; 14-18 weeks → ROI ~3.9:1 → Do in months 2-3

**Tier 2: Consider Rebuilding (Medium ROI; Moderate Cost)**
4. Legacy Report Format: $120K cost; $750K at-risk; 12-16 weeks → ROI ~6.2:1 → Deprioritize; offer custom services budget ($50K) to affected 5 customers instead; ROI improves
5. Custom Workflow Automation: $200K cost; $1.2M at-risk; 16-20 weeks → ROI ~6:1 → Deprioritize initially; offer 50% discount on replacement to offset friction; revisit if customers request

**Tier 3: Do Not Rebuild (Poor ROI; High Cost)**
6. Custom API Endpoints: $150K cost; $1.2M at-risk (but spread across 12 customers; real ROI is lower because not all will defect) → Consider API bridge instead ($50K; gives 70% of the benefit with 1/3 the cost)
7. Embedded Dashboard Component: $250K cost; $600K at-risk (but spread across 3 customers; 250K/3 = $83K per customer; too high) → Offer these 3 customers custom services budget ($80K) instead; cheaper and more customer-friendly

**Total Rebuild Cost (Tier 1 + Tier 2): ~$530K**
**Revenue at Risk (if no rebuilds): ~$6.45M** (sum of all cohorts)
**Revenue Protected (with Tier 1 + 2): ~$5.5M** (assuming 80-90% of customers in these segments migrate)
**Net ROI: ~10:1**

This is a **no-brainer economically**. Rebuild Tier 1 immediately; it costs $210K and protects $2.3M in revenue. Do it.
```

**Key insights from feature dependency:**

1. **Most niche features are cheap to rebuild.** The XML export costs $30K; the FTP connector costs $130K. These are not big bets. Compare to losing $800K and $1.5M in annual recurring revenue. Rebuilding is economically rational.

2. **Some features are not worth rebuilding (Embedded Dashboard).** They cost too much ($250K) relative to the customer base (3 customers). For these, offer alternative solutions: custom services budget, white-label consulting, or accept churn. Better to lose $600K in revenue from 3 customers than to spend $250K on a rebuild + 20 weeks of engineering time.

3. **API bridges are cheaper than full rebuilds.** For Custom API Endpoints, instead of rebuilding the entire deprecated API, build a bridge layer that translates old API calls into new API calls. Cost is 1/3 of full rebuild; customers get 70% of the benefit.

4. **Customer service budgets are your secret weapon.** Instead of rebuilding the Embedded Dashboard feature, offer the 3 affected customers a custom services budget ($80K per customer) to build what they need on their own or with their own contractor. Cost to you is 1/3 of the rebuild; they get exactly what they need; relationship is preserved.

---

#### **Action 0.3: Defection Risk Scoring (Days 5-12)**

For each customer, estimate the probability they'll defect during the sunset period.

```
DEFECTION RISK SCORING MODEL

Customer | Cohort | Feature Dependency | Rebuild Status | Switching Cost (Integrations) | Contract Length | Account Health (NPS/Engagement) | Competitor Interest | Defection Risk Score | Risk Level | Action
---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---
Acme Corp | Pragmatist | Low | N/A | Low | 3-year deal (locked in) | Good (8/10) | Low | 15% | Low | Monitor; light incentive for early migration
TechCorp | Feature-Dependent | FTP Connector | Rebuilding (Tier 1) | Medium | 1-year deal (expires in 8 months) | Neutral (5/10) | Medium | 45% | Medium | Rebuild FTP feature; offer 20% discount on replacement for 2-year extension
GlobalInc | Deep-Integrator | Custom APIs (3 custom integrations) | Evaluating bridge | Very High | 1-year deal (month-to-month after) | Deteriorating (4/10) | High (competitor actively pursuing) | 70% | High | Immediate action: offer custom services budget ($100K) + free migration consulting + 25% discount; lock in 2-year deal
StartupXYZ | Pragmatist | None | N/A | Low | 1-year (new customer; expires in 11 months) | Excellent (9/10) | None | 10% | Low | Smooth migration path; no discount needed (happy customer)
EnterpriseA | Feature-Dependent | Custom Workflow | Deprioritized (Tier 2) | Medium | 1-year (month-to-month after) | Good (7/10) | Medium | 55% | Medium | Offer 30% discount on replacement + free custom services ($30K) to offset migration friction
MidMarketB | Vendor-Agnostic | None | N/A | Low | 1-year (1 month to renewal) | Neutral (5/10) | Very High (competitor undercut us by 20%) | 65% | High | Immediate action: 25% discount for 2-year replacement deal; lock in before they shop
...

---

**Scoring Methodology:**

Base Risk = 50% (assume all customers have moderate defection risk during sunset)

Adjustments:
- Feature Dependency:
  - None: -10%
  - Covered by Replacement: -5%
  - Niche but rebuilding: -15%
  - Niche and not rebuilding: +30%
- Switching Cost (Integrations):
  - Low: -5%
  - Medium: 0%
  - High: +20%
  - Very High: +35%
- Contract Lock:
  - Long-term (2+ years): -15%
  - Medium-term (1-2 years): -5%
  - Short-term / month-to-month: +10%
- Account Health:
  - Excellent (NPS 8-10): -10%
  - Good (NPS 6-7): -5%
  - Neutral (NPS 4-5): 0%
  - Poor (NPS <4): +10%
- Competitor Activity:
  - None: -10%
  - Medium: 0%
  - High: +20%

Final Risk Score = Base (50%) + adjustments

---

**Risk Buckets:**

- **High (>60%):** Immediate retention action required. These are your defection risks. Personalized offer + relationship management + possible custom solutions.
- **Medium (40-60%):** Proactive retention. Standard incentive + clear migration path + regular check-ins.
- **Low (<40%):** Monitor. Light incentive + standard communication. May not need special treatment.

**Expected Outcomes by Risk Bucket:**

- High Risk (15-20% of base): 40-50% will defect without intervention; 20-30% will defect even with intervention; 50-60% will stay if you offer strong incentives + custom solutions
- Medium Risk (35-45% of base): 15-25% will defect without intervention; 5-10% will defect with intervention; 75-85% will stay with standard incentives
- Low Risk (40-50% of base): 5-10% will defect without intervention; <5% will defect with any intervention; 90%+ will stay with standard communication

**Revenue Impact:**

Assuming 1000 customers distributed across risk buckets:
- High Risk (180 customers, median $150K): $27M revenue at risk; assume 45% defect = $12.15M loss
- Medium Risk (400 customers, median $80K): $32M revenue at risk; assume 20% defect = $6.4M loss
- Low Risk (420 customers, median $50K): $21M revenue at risk; assume 7% defect = $1.47M loss

**Without intervention: $20M revenue loss (33% of legacy revenue)**
**With targeted intervention (see action 1.2): $5-8M revenue loss (8-13% of legacy revenue)**
```

**Key insights from defection risk:**

1. **Most defection happens in the first 12 months; it's concentrated in High-Risk customers.** If you can retain 60% of your High-Risk customers (through custom solutions, discounts, migration tooling), you save ~$7M in revenue. This is where your retention effort should be concentrated.

2. **Contract lock is your friend.** Customers with 2+ year contracts are far less likely to defect (they're legally and practically stuck). If you can convert high-risk customers to 2-year renewal deals during the sunset period, you lock in their revenue even if they're unhappy about the transition.

3. **Competitor activity is a strong defection signal.** If competitors are actively pursuing your customers, they're probably already evaluating alternatives. Get in front of this immediately with a strong retention offer.

4. **Poor account health + short contract = immediate risk.** Customers with NPS <4 and month-to-month contracts are likely gone within 6 months. Don't spend money trying to save them; focus on customers with good relationships (NPS 6+) who are at-risk due to feature/switching cost issues (these are recoverable).

---

### **Phase 1: Redesign the Replacement Product (Weeks 2-16)**

While your diagnostic is running, your product team needs to close the feature gaps that lock customers into legacy.

#### **Action 1.1: Feature Rebuild Roadmap (Days 8-20)**

Take the Tier 1 and Tier 2 feature list and schedule rebuilds.

```
FEATURE REBUILD ROADMAP: 24-WEEK SPRINT

Timeline | Feature | Customer Cohort | Revenue at Risk | Rebuild Effort | Owner | Dependencies | Launch Target | Migration Trigger
---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---
**Weeks 2-9 (Immediate)** | XML Export Compatibility | Feature-Dependent (8 customers) | $800K | 6 weeks | Backend Engineer A | None | Week 10 | Email: "XML export now available in replacement"
**Weeks 2-16 (Immediate)** | FTP Upload Connector | Feature-Dependent (15 customers) | $1.5M | 12 weeks | Backend Engineer A + DevOps | Infrastructure setup | Week 17 | Email: "FTP connector now available; we're ready to help you migrate"
**Weeks 4-10 (Concurrent)** | Real-time Webhooks Performance Optimization | Feature-Dependent (7 customers) + Deep-Integrator overlap | $700K | 8 weeks | Backend Engineer B | None | Week 11 | Targeted outreach: "We've improved webhook latency to match your real-time requirements"
**Weeks 11-20 (Secondary)** | Custom Report Builder | Feature-Dependent (5 customers) + Pragmatists | $750K + expansion | 12 weeks | Product Engineer C + Designer | Backend features from week 10 | Week 21 | Product launch + case study
**Weeks 13-28 (Contingency)** | Custom Workflow Automation Engine | Feature-Dependent (6 customers) | $1.2M | 16 weeks | Product Engineer D + Engineer E | Architecture review | Week 29 | Targeted outreach; offer custom implementation services
**Weeks 15-27 (Nice-to-Have)** | API Bridge Layer (for Custom API Endpoints) | Feature-Dependent (12 customers) | $1.2M (but 40% customer overlap; real at-risk is $720K) | 10 weeks | Backend Engineer F | Replacement API finalization | Week 28 | Technical documentation; webinar for early adopters

---

**Feature Launch Sequencing:**

**Month 1 (Weeks 2-4): Announce Rebuild Plan**
- Internal: Communicate to product team that rebuild is happening; get buy-in
- External: Email to Feature-Dependent customers: "We heard you. We're rebuilding [features X, Y, Z] in the replacement. Here's our timeline. We're committed to making your migration as smooth as possible."
- Messaging: **Inversion of the typical sunset message.** Instead of "we're killing legacy," say "we're bringing your favorite features to the new product."

**Months 2-3 (Weeks 9-13): Launch Tier 1 Features**
- XML Export goes live (week 10)
- Real-time Webhooks optimization goes live (week 11)
- Trigger: Email every Feature-Dependent customer who depends on these features: "Your feature is now available in replacement. Here's a guide to migrate. We're offering 20% discount for 2-year contract to make the economics work for you."

**Months 3-4 (Weeks 14-17): Launch Tier 1.5 Features**
- FTP Connector goes live (week 17)
- Trigger: Email to 15 FTP-dependent customers + announcement in customer newsletter

**Months 4-6 (Weeks 17-27): Launch Tier 2 Features**
- Custom Report Builder (week 21)
- API Bridge (week 28)
- Trigger: Staggered outreach; customer success team does personalized calls

**Contingency (Weeks 28+): Tier 2 Advanced Features**
- Custom Workflow Automation (week 29)
- Only if multiple customers request it; otherwise deprioritize
```

**Key principles for feature rebuild:**

1. **Launch features *before* you push migration.** Don't tell Feature-Dependent customers to migrate until their critical features are available in the replacement. Messaging order matters: "We built your feature" → "It's live" → "Here's why you should migrate" → "Here's the incentive."

2. **Use feature launches as migration triggers.** When XML export goes live, that's your permission to email the 8 customers who depend on it. You're not pushing sunset; you're announcing "your barrier to migration is gone."

3. **Build migration velocity into the product.** Make XML export easy to use; make the FTP connector "just work"; reduce friction. The replacement should feel like a lateral move for Feature-Dependent customers, not a downgrade.

4. **Communicate rebuilds to all customers, not just Feature-Dependent.** In your quarterly newsletter, announce: "Based on customer feedback, we're adding [feature X] to the new product." This reinforces to Pragmatists that the replacement is getting better; it gives you credibility; it extends your migration timeline (more people are willing to wait for the replacement if they know it's improving).

---

#### **Action 1.2: Replacement Product Roadmap Overhaul (Days 10-20)**

Beyond feature rebuilds, the replacement product needs to be actively marketed and improved *during the sunset period*.

The mistake most companies make: They focus all energy on legacy sunset and forget to market/improve the replacement. Result: The replacement feels stagnant; customers see it as an inferior product they're being forced into.

Counter-strategy: **Heavy investment in replacement product during legacy sunset.**

```
REPLACEMENT PRODUCT INVESTMENT: 24-MONTH ROADMAP

Quarter | Investment Area | Why | Expected Outcome | Customer Narrative
---|---|---|---|---
**Q1** | Feature Rebuilds (see 1.1) | Close feature gaps that lock customers into legacy | 3-4 high-value features launched | "The new product now has everything you need"
**Q1-Q2** | Performance / Stability | Replacement needs to be *faster* and *more reliable* than legacy to justify migration | Latency reduced by 30%; uptime improved to 99.99% | "The new product is better performance"
**Q2** | UX Overhaul (New Features) | Replacement should have *visibly better UX* than legacy; new features should look better, feel better | 5-6 new UX features; 2-3 entirely new capabilities | "The new product gives you superpowers"
**Q3** | Integrations Expansion | Deep-Integrators are locked in by API / integrations. Add 10-15 new integrations to replacement | 10-15 new partnerships; community API program launches | "The new product connects to everything"
**Q3-Q4** | Migration Tooling | Build scripts, templates, and tools to make Deep-Integrator migrations easy | Data migration tooling; API bridge; custom integration templates | "Migrating is easy; we'll help you"
**Q4** | Advanced Analytics / Insights | Power Users want intelligence. Add AI-driven insights, predictive features | 3-4 AI-powered features | "The new product is smarter"

---

**Communication Strategy During Rebuild:**

Every quarter, *publicly* announce replacement product improvements.

**Q1 Announcement (Weeks 1-2):**
```
Blog Post: "The New Product Just Got Your Favorite Features"

Subject: We Built What You Asked For

Body:
"We listened to your feedback. Many of you use [legacy product] because of specific capabilities: XML exports, FTP connectors, real-time data feeds. 

Today, we're excited to announce that all three are now available in the new product. 

Why does this matter? Because it means you can finally upgrade to the product we've been building for the past 2 years, without losing any capability. And you'll gain [10 new features] that don't exist in the legacy version.

Here's what's new in the replacement product:
- XML export: Available today
- Real-time webhooks: 40% faster latency
- FTP connector: In beta; generally available in 3 weeks
